comparison: Both evaluate PVRL4 genomic amplification claims (C9, C36). OpenEval accepts the database analysis and published citations as supporting amplification. Peer reviewers explicitly challenge this, noting the cited database 'does not distinguish high-level amplification from single copy gain' and that Oncomine data shows no cases with HER2-level amplification, concluding copy number evidence does not strongly support PVRL4 as a driver oncogene.

Both address in vivo xenograft experiments (C29-C32). OpenEval finds the tumor growth inhibition data with shRNA and antibody approaches well-supported. Peer reviewers acknowledge findings but express concern about generalizability, noting experiments used cell lines with 'particularly high levels' of PVRL4 and requesting additional experiments in cell lines with lower expression levels to determine broader applicability.

Both evaluate PVRL4-mediated cell clustering and anchorage-independent growth mechanism (C15-C19, C46). Strong agreement: OpenEval finds multiple converging lines of evidence support the claims. Peer reviewers explicitly praise the work as 'elegant' and affirm that 'PVRL4 appears to be capable of mediating anchorage-independent growth' with strong aggregation effects.

Both evaluate signaling pathway mechanisms (C21-C25, C44). OpenEval finds the mass spectrometry, co-IP, knockdown, and pharmacological inhibition data well-supported. Peer reviewers do not challenge the mechanistic findings and accept the PVRL4-PVRL1-integrin signaling pathway as part of their overall positive assessment of the mechanistic work.

Both evaluate the ORFeome screen and PVRL4 identification (C7, C12). OpenEval finds the screen methodology and validation experiments directly support the claims. Peer reviewers explicitly praise 'the elegant ORFeome screen to investigate anchorage-independent growth' and accept PVRL4 as a validated hit from the screen.

Both evaluate structure-function experiments with deletion mutants (C13, C14, C20). OpenEval finds the extracellular domain necessity and sufficiency well-demonstrated. Peer reviewers do not challenge these findings and accept them as part of the overall mechanistic characterization they praise.

Both address PVRL4 dependency in cancer cells (C26-C28). OpenEval finds focal amplification, functional assays with shRNAs, and rescue experiments support dependency claims. Peer reviewers acknowledge findings but question generalizability beyond high-expressing cell lines, requesting experiments in cells with lower PVRL4 expression to establish broader dependency.

Both evaluate antibody mechanism of action (C33, C34, C49). OpenEval finds ADCC assays and immunohistochemistry appropriately rule out Fc-mediated immune mechanisms. Peer reviewers do not explicitly challenge these negative control experiments but their overall UNCERTAIN status for the therapeutic approach reflects concerns about generalizability rather than mechanism.

Both address therapeutic implications (C10). OpenEval finds rescue experiments and functional data support PVRL4 as a therapeutic target. Peer reviewers acknowledge 'antibodies to PVRL4 would seem to be a viable therapeutic strategy in a cancer with very high levels' but emphasize need for 'more analysis to determine how often human breast cancers utilize the PVRL4 pathway oncogenically.'

Both evaluate PVRL4 overexpression and clinical associations (C37, C43). OpenEval accepts the cited clinical studies as supporting overexpression claims. Peer reviewers acknowledge 'many breast cancers seem to over express PVRL4 compared to normal breast epithelium' and accept the clinical associations, though they note overexpression is weaker evidence than amplification.

Both address clinical relevance claims (C41). OpenEval finds the cited clinical studies provide appropriate context. Peer reviewers do not challenge the clinical associations cited in the literature, accepting them as background context while focusing their concerns on the strength of amplification evidence.

Both address EMT marker analysis (C35). OpenEval finds Western blot data showing unchanged E-cadherin and vimentin appropriately addresses safety concerns. Peer reviewers do not explicitly challenge this finding, but their overall uncertainty about therapeutic applicability encompasses concerns about effects beyond the high-expressing cell lines tested.

Both address increased cell-cell adhesion with oncogenic perturbations (C45). OpenEval finds clustering assay data with multiple oncogenic perturbations supports this as a general feature. Peer reviewers do not challenge this finding and it aligns with their acceptance of the aggregation and anchorage-independence mechanisms.

Both evaluate the central mechanistic conclusion (C8). OpenEval finds the convergence of multiple experimental results supports the PVRL4-mediated cell-cell contact mechanism. Peer reviewers explicitly accept this mechanism, praising the elegant demonstration that PVRL4 mediates anchorage-independent growth through cell aggregation.

OpenEval evaluates background claims about epithelial cancer biology (C1-C3) and finds them well-established with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found; these introductory claims were not specifically addressed by reviewers.

OpenEval evaluates prior work linking cell-cell aggregation to metastatic behavior (C4-C6) and finds appropriate citations support these claims. No corresponding peer review evaluation found; reviewers did not specifically address these background literature claims.

OpenEval evaluates the proposed 'zipper' molecular mechanism (C47) and correctly identifies it as explicitly speculative, lacking direct experimental evidence. No corresponding peer review evaluation found; reviewers did not specifically address this speculative mechanistic model.

OpenEval evaluates the interpretive model about PVRL4-driven contacts enabling matrix-independent signaling (C48) and finds it well-supported by experimental data. No corresponding peer review evaluation found; reviewers did not specifically address this integrative model claim.

Peer reviewers evaluate therapeutic potential (C10, C11) and acknowledge viability for high-expressing cancers but emphasize need for more analysis of how often cancers utilize the PVRL4 pathway. OpenEval R9 partially overlaps with C10 but peer R4 uniquely addresses C11 and broader therapeutic generalizability concerns not captured in a single OpenEval result.
